utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe, in the last day or two, there was some discussion about the admissibility of some photographic exhibits and also a directive from the Chamber to produce a list of those photographic exhibits and the dates or approximate dates when they were taken, and then a suggestion to get together with coordinating counsel, Mr. Pavkovic, and see if we could narrow the issues. We have done that, Mr. Pavkovic and I have met this morning and have narrowed the issues, and we wanted to simply announce that to the Court and to seek the Court's guidance as to when would be an appropriate time to deal with those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you, so how many photographs are still not agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If the Court has in front of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- the index, I can read out the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: P-15 through P-22, all of those inclusive, and then one more, P-24, and I believe, and Mr. Pavkovic can confirm that or correct me if I'm wrong, that would be the extent of the photographs at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I can only confirm what the Prosecutor has said, and it is the Defence counsel's standpoint that these photographs, these exhibits, are to be contested. We consider that these exhibits, if you will allow me to summarise our standpoint -- Your Honour, may I proceed? The Defence maintains that these exhibits cannot be connected either by time or by place with the events pertaining to the indictment. As we know, these photographs might have been taken, unfortunately, at any place in Bosnia during this war. These are the reasons why the Defence cannot accept what the Prosecutor considers to be evidence and something that, according to the Prosecutor, should confirm his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think most of these photographs, or probably all of them, were taken by Colonel Watters; is that correct? Or produced but also -- yes, produced by him --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But taken -- I thought he had himself taken or some of his soldiers had taken those photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, either he or his soldiers had taken the photographs on the date specified in the index. I believe he said he may have taken the photograph number 24, the one of the anti-aircraft gun, but my recollection is that he said, if he didn't, it was common practice for his soldiers to take photographs of big weapons in the area during that time period. I believe he also testified that he was in Bosnia from the period of February through May of '93, and all these photographs at issue were taken during that time period, and therefore, we believe are quite relevant to the issues in this case. I might also add that it appears to me that the primary objection of the Defence is not necessarily the admissibility of these photographs, that is, whether they were properly identified by a competent witness as being fair and accurate, but a broader objection as to their pertinence to the legal or factual issues of this case, and I think that is an argument that is premature since the evidence in this case is still at the preliminary stage and, in any event, I think that's something the Court can take into consideration at the end of the case, to determine what evidence, if any, it should consider in determining the guilt or innocence of any of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have just decided that all of them will be admitted into evidence. They were taken either by Colonel Watters or his soldiers, and he testified in court to this effect, so we don't have any doubt about their authenticity. As to the direct relevance, if any, to the facts which are in issue here, then we will, of course, decide on this matter later on. But for the time being, they are admitted into evidence. So we may now move on to the cross-examination of our witness, and I would like to turn to Mr. Pavkovic to ask him whether he could briefly indicate to us who is going to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Petar Puliselic will be the first Defence counsel to cross-examine the witness. He will be followed by Ranko Radovic and then by Mrs. Jandranka Slokovic-Glumac and the others will then see whether all the essential questions have been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Puliselic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, do you know to whom you made statements before arriving at the International Tribunal in connection with the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know to what organisation or to what service you made a statement or statements in connection with the events in Ahmici. You made a statement this year, which we have in our files, so, please, can you tell us to whom you made this statement, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: At my police station to the investigators investigating war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you perhaps told what you were supposed to say and what persons you were supposed to mention?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not told who I should mention. I know who I should mention, and I went through hell, and that's what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what AID is, A-I-D, what this stands for?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you why your statement was made as late as 1998, that is, five years after the event?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, as a refugee, you arrived in Ahmici from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who drove you away from your house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: We were driven away by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about what time did you arrive in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I left Prijedor on the 22nd of August. We spent some time in Travnik. And then I went to Vitez where I spent some time in a children's holiday centre, two nights, and then, sometime in early September --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's when you arrived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Ahmici by yourself?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a wife and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your intention? Was it your intention to remain in Ahmici permanently or was it only a temporary solution?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I considered it a temporary solution because I wanted to go back where I had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps how many other refugees from Prijedor arrived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you make an estimate?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: A few families, but some of them went abroad and some stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other refugees from other places arrive in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were people from Jajce, from Tjentiste, from eastern Bosnia, people from Karaule, from Visegrad, and some other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not consider staying in Ahmici to be a long-term solution, that you intended to go back to the place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in the statement you made to AID, which is the Muslim Intelligence, you said that it was your intention to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I couldn't get the necessary documents to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the obstacle to your getting these documents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: You needed a lot of documents, a lot of things, and I didn't have anything with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you had not joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone promise to give you documents if you did them a favour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody promised me anything, nor did I ask for anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in this court that you were familiar with the location of the Papic house.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I passed by quite a few times as I was going toward Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who inhabited the house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Ivo Papic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight. I knew Dragan best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him? Did you ever talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I only knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know this was Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know because other people saw him as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in this court that you had met Dragan Papic on two occasions several days before the main conflict and that he was wearing a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you had also seen him previously in that black uniform?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was before the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you had once seen him carrying a sniper?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether you know something about weapons.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know what a sniper is, I know what an automatic rifle is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know it was a sniper? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it has an optical device on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what an Ustasha flag looks like?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that it was something black, a black flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Croatia, they put black flags on the house of a deceased. What kind of flags did you see? You mentioned it. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a big checkerboard flag flying from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that flag always there, the checkerboard flag, or was it there only when they were celebrating a holiday on feast days and so on?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. But when I passed by, I saw it, and that's how I described it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of them, because they were all civilians and none of them were in the army where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But didn't you go further abroad from your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a little, but I was full of fear. I didn't like moving about a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the Muslims carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mehrudin Bilic, nicknamed Mehro?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he had a weapon in his house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Hazrudin Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puliselic. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a photograph yesterday, and when your finger happened to stop at a place which you could not identify, he told you to put a circle around it and that you would be doing a good deed. I'm asking you, do you know what it is that you put a circle around?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to repeat it. What is it that you encircled in response to a request from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked to encircle the house in which I stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking because that was something else that he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to make things easier, would it be possible to have the exhibit again, to show the photograph again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the photograph is shown again to Mr. Rizvanovic, may I ask him whether, in the meantime, that is, since yesterday's testimony, he discussed this point with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then let him show on this photograph the Papic house and then let him show the house where he was staying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we can't hear the witness. He's not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, often it is difficult to orient yourself in this photograph. The best way to see it is to turn it around for Mr. Rizvanovic. It may be strange to us, but he can orient himself much better on this photograph if it's turned around. That's the only explanation I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can we see the witness pointing, please, on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is where I stayed, this is where you have to go forward. Somewhere here. Here somewhere. Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that? What is that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Papic house. If you go this way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you show it to us exactly, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the path, isn't it, going to Vitez, isn't it? Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see. Could the technical booth please show us what the witness is pointing to because I can't see what it is that he is showing.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is, it is this house. This house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I passed along this road many times and I saw his house here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is his house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you put a circle around it with a red marker?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please use a red marker to put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe a blue marker would be better so that we can see the difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you have a blue marker?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: It should be here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put a circle, please, a circle. A cross. All right.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: These were these houses. It should be here somewhere. And up here is the road going --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't put a cross but put a circle around the cross. Fine. Thank you. You were saying something about black uniforms and a black flag. My learned colleague started asking you questions about that, but let me continue. What does a black flag mean to you? Will you please explain to us whether it was all black, plain black, or had some other indicators on it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I looked at it from the road, I couldn't notice the details except that it was quite long and it was black, but the checkerboard --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leave aside the checkerboard. I'm asking you about the black flag. Did it have any signs on it except being a piece of black cloth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't notice that from the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your association when you saw this black flag? What did it mean to you in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't even know what it meant, but later, I learnt it was the Ustasha flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is a Ustasha flag, according to you. Do you know what a Ustasha flag looked like?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, do you know what an Ustasha flag looks like? Do you or do you not know? Answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: It had symbols, but I couldn't see that. I could just see that it was black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Does a black flag mean an Ustasha flag to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're talking about an Ustasha flag, I'm asking you, can you tell us what an Ustasha flag looks like? Do you know what it looks like or not? I think the majority of people in this hall don't know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not old enough to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But an Ustasha flag was never a black flag. You said that Papic had a black uniform on. What, in your mind, did that black uniform represent?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Ustashas wore black flags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, they didn't. Was it all Ustashas or just a separate unit of Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five years after the events, you made the statement to the AID agency. How actually did you get in touch with AID? Did they come to look for you or did you yourself report or how was this contact established? How did they learn about you five years after the events? And you were questioned at a time when a whole team of investigators of the International Tribunal was there, so how come they didn't interview you but, rather, the AID agency?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they found me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me how it went? Did they call you or did you go yourself?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the AID office yourself or did somebody come to fetch you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: They came home to my house, they knew I had been there and that I had survived the genocide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they learned about it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was registered with the Red Cross and then they inquired where people had been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was some time ago, but quite recently, they came to my house. I can't remember the date because my brain is not really working properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we are still fresh. This is only the morning. What will happen in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering what I went through, even this is a wonder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you about that. I just want to know what happened. You said that in the month of October, the inhabitants of Ahmici put up a barricade on the road and would not allow HVO soldiers to pass. What can you tell us about that? Why did they build a barricade? Did they do this on their own initiative or did they receive an order to erect this barricade?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know on whose initiative it was done. I just know that it was because when there was that clash in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It's a slang word the witness is using which we in Zagreb also use to mean "clash" or "chaos."

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't allow them to pass. Then they crossed to the hill of Hrasno and then they attacked Ahmici. But this was a smaller-scale conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at the time a Muslim young man was killed. Do you know whether any Croats were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but I know that a 16-year-old Muslim was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that no one introduced you to Croats and that you didn't have any particular contact with Croats.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned the name of Dragan Papic in AID, did you yourself provide the name or did the people from AID suggest it to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you link the name to the person?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, my name is Ranko Radovic. How did you learn what my name was? Did somebody point me to you or what?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I first came, I was staying with Bilic Hijadet, and Bilic's house and Papic's house are very close, and this is how I learned that that was Papic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in AID and interviewed about Papic Dragan, were any photographs shown to you on the basis of which you might be able to identify the person that you considered to be Papic Dragan?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't give me anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just mentioned the name and they didn't ask you to point to the person you considered to be Papic Dragan on the basis of photographs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: But why should they when I knew him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just asking you whether you were shown any photographs for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were one of the more cautious people, and you said that on the 15th of April, 1993 -- there's a misprint here. It says '92. I suppose it should be '93 -- that you reached the mosque and that you warned them that you had seen Croats moving out. Another friend told you that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noticed something yourself and another friend told you something. My question is: Which people did you warn near the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: People were walking around. I suppose we had agreed that we should let each other know as soon as we noticed anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly about what time of day was this on the 15th of April when you told people about the danger? I know that you weren't wearing a watch, but roughly what time was it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was just before dark fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that the local people didn't believe, didn't believe you. And how did they explain this lack of belief in your warnings?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before all these things had happened, relations were good among them. They had nice relations among the people, in between the period of the first aggression and this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't understand anything you're saying. You came to warn these people around the mosque of danger signals?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any of the persons that you talked to about what you had noticed and that there was a danger sign? Will you please remember the surnames too?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Senko, I can't remember his surname, his house is right next to the mosque, and Vehbija, I can't remember his name. He was there too. His house is also next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they made light of what you were saying to them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they discuss what you had told them with others?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps. We stayed there talking for a while and then each one went to his own home to see what he should do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said two things that were contradictory yesterday, so let's clarify that. You said yesterday that you didn't sleep all night, but you also said that you were awakened by the first shot. When sleeping, how could you be awakened?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was lying down. I was dozing. I wasn't sleeping properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were half awake, so to speak. Half awake, half asleep. Is that acceptable as a definition?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were neither awake nor asleep, how then could you identify the position from which the first shot came when it actually woke you up?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the shot and I jumped up immediately and I knew where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the sound, you identified it by the sound; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just saying --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see the bullet?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you can't see a bullet. How can you see a bullet?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to the sound?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did you ever go to Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a local inhabitant, so I don't really know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the central part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went through the woods, if that is what is called Grabovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who owns which house among the Croats and Muslims in Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went there rarely, but I knew roughly who were the Croats and who were the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the roofs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well then, how did you know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the neighbours would say these are Catholic homes and these are Muslim homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you the names, or did they just tell you these were Catholic and these were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would give me the names, but that wasn't of any interest to me because I was a refugee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't intend to stay anyway, so that didn't interest you. Could you give us the name of any individual Croat whose house you remember up there in the central part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know the house of the person who had a shop. What was his name? Kupreskic, yes. We would go to buy something there, the man who had the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were several of their houses there around the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the owners of the houses near the shop?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Vlatko, Zoran, and Mirjan. Those were those houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you remember them.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it from the stories, from the conversations that we had when we went to the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far the Kupreskic house is from the place where you were that morning; that is, to be more precise, from the Bilic house as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not far, but I'm not very good at measurement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you went on foot, how many minutes would it take you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not far to go to the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not far, but it needs some time.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch to measure, so I don't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever pass by those other houses apart from the one in which the shop was?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did sometimes go to Upper Ahmici, but I moved around very little, very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're going to Upper Ahmici, do you pass by those houses? Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how -- what I was told when I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name the person in Upper Ahmici that you went to visit when you went along that road?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name? (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Radovic. Again, the interpreters are asking whether you could make a break, have a break between questions and answers so that we can follow the interpretation. Otherwise, the transcript will not be accurate and we can't follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us the first and last name of the man that you went to visit in upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to visit (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you again, are you sure that when you went to Upper Ahmici, you passed by the Kupreskic house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you're going up, you go a bit to the left, and I was told that those were the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have a map now for me to show you so that you could show us, but we will show the Trial Chamber the photograph or the map which will show that you do not pass by the Kupreskic houses to go to Upper Ahmici. Tell us, (redacted) have a house in Upper Ahmici? Was he living there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was staying with someone. I didn't ask him whether that was his house or not. I just stopped by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Upper Ahmici, you went to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it was his house. I had a coffee with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to a particular place to see (redacted). What would you say if we told you that (redacted) is not in Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: He is. He's there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us say that is so. Tell me now, in connection with the unit which was allegedly attacking, what did you hear about it? Who among the Croats attacked Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but when you were interviewed in AID, you said something special. Do you know or don't you know which unit was attacking?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing more than that. All you know is that it was the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some Jokers were participating too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that they were participating?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the local people. That a unit from Busovaca had come and some other people from Herzegovina when there was the attack at Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel make a pause, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You should slow down. Otherwise, we can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please identify the person that you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it from the local inhabitants. I didn't take note of their names. The people were talking about it, the locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know the locals by name, but you do know the names of the Croats with whom you had no contact.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I was walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But surely you were walking around near the Croats too, surely.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was there in Ahmici that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell me the name of the local who told you, who identified the unit that was attacking. Because, you see, it's a bit strange to me, because in your statement, you name the Croats with whom you did not socialise and you can't name the locals with whom you did socialise.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, there was Senko there, and there were others, Edzo, I heard this from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were making the statement in AID, were you shown anybody's photograph, the photograph of any Croat for the purposes of identification?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Mirjan mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirjan? He's Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you hear his name?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it when I came to the shop. They referred to the Kupreskics, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has Vlatko Kupreskic's shop have to do with Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was told that Mirjan was living just behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the peasants, the farmers, they know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise Mirjan in person?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recognise Zoran?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them in your life?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I may have passed by them, but I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything from personal experience what they were doing on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 16th of April? I heard what I have already told you about, who had participated in that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what you said, I'm interested in what you saw and what you heard?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but not well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on television?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no TV set, so I couldn't watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. Before -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you will allow me one second. Before we move on to other legal counsel, may I call upon all legal counsel, Defence counsel, to refrain from any ironical comments or remarks. This is not proper in court. We will no longer allow any counsel of Prosecution to make such comments about witnesses. This is quite unacceptable. Yes, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these words, Mr. President. I would like to ask for some clarification as to the order in the proceedings. Yesterday, when I was carrying out the examination-in-chief of Mr. Rizvanovic, I limited myself to three items in the written statements. They were points which seemed very important to me. And I didn't want to waste the Tribunal's time with other elements that were of minor relevance. I do not query the relevance of the questions raised by the two Defence counsel, but I have the feeling that many of the questions raised were outside the scope of the questions I put yesterday during the examination-in-chief. I also had the feeling that, especially Mr. Radovic, put a lot of questions related to Dragan Papic, although he's not Dragan Papic's counsel. I am aware of Rule 90(H) of the Rules and I had the feelings that the principle expressed in that rule is that the cross-examination should remain within the scope of the examination-in-chief. You pointed out in these last few days that there are also exceptions indicated in the Rules, but it is important for us, when we prepare and carry out examination-in-chief, it is important for us to know whether the witness is going to be questioned on all of the elements to be found in written statements disclosed to the Defence. In this case, in this instance, I wonder whether we should limit ourselves to those points which are relevant to us. This is the very issue I wanted to put to you. I was seeking some clarification from the Court because I had some questions as to the way this Rule was implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, but I'm going to discuss this with my colleagues, the Defence is allowed to put questions related to the credibility of the witness, and that is a wide scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So they are entitled to check whether the witness is credible so they're allowed to go beyond the questions you raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Many questions were put as to the credibility of the witness. That's fine. I have no objection to that. That's quite legitimate for Defence counsel to do so. But I had the feeling, especially listening to the questions raised by Mr. Radovic, more so at the beginning of his cross-examination, that many areas were broached which were not areas that I had gone into in examination-in-chief. I'm wondering whether that is the rule, but I'm also wondering as to the scope of implementation and the use the Court intends to make of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I personally feel that when there is a doubt, we must take the rights of the Defence into account. So if there is any doubt, the advantage should go to the Defence which would raise relevant questions. But, of course, if you have the feeling that a question is being raised which is of no relevance because it goes beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief to start with, and also beyond the scope of credibility, then you are allowed to raise objections. But I personally would be more inclined to give the advantage to the Defence because they are allowed to test the statements made by the witness, and I think that can't be established just in abstract terms. My colleagues agree with me so much more so that we could add as an argument, as a further argument, that at this stage, the Court is not in a position to assess the relevance of a question. There may be questions put by the Defence for reasons that we're not aware of. So it may be that the Defence might want to raise questions which are relevant for the Defence of their client. However, in the future, if there are objections raised by the Prosecution, we could see whether there are any doubts as to the relevance of questions raised by the Defence when the Court would be entitled to ask the Defence why they think that the question is relevant for them. That's the method we could decide to have. But in principle, we would be rather inclined to take due account of the rights of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We shall indeed comply with your views, but I had another question. Mr. Radovic raised many questions related to Dragan Papic, although he's not Dragan Papic's counsel. I didn't want to butt in, but questions might be of relevance, questions he asked, but it was not up to Mr. Radovic to put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the questioning was performed by Mr. Papic -- the first cross-examination was done by Mr. Papic's counsel. The question of the black flag and the black uniform is not just a question that refers to Mr. Papic but Ustasha uniforms and Ustasha symbols do not refer only to Papic. The issue of Ustasha insignia will turn up quite often during the proceedings, and as I said, most of the people involved in these proceedings do not know what Ustasha uniforms and insignia looked like. In Zagreb, we will get a book which shows what these uniforms and insignia look like, but I declare here that a black uniform was the uniform of a special unit of the Ustasha army which was called the Black Legion, and the Ustasha flag was never black, it was red, white, and blue with a letter "U" and the Croatian coat of arms. So one story is being told here, but the reality is different, so I'm just trying to show that people are talking about things which they do not know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I think you made a good point. I think you're right in saying that this question was indeed relevant to the credibility of the witness and did not merely refer to Papic, to accused Dragan Papic. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that Mr. Moskowitz can help as far as this is concerned because the common law rule, at least in the United Kingdom, is that counsel is not prevented from asking questions about another co-defendant. Whether it's wise to ask questions involving a co-defendant of course is another matter. But I don't think there can be a rule which prevents counsel as it were encroaching on another counsel's case and on what may involve a co-defendant, and the example which was just given is one which may be of general relevance, although in this particular part of the evidence, it related to one witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour? I agree, in the American system, there is no rule that would prohibit co-counsel from asking questions, even if unwise questions, that would pertain to a co-defendant. I think our concern here is having six Defence attorneys in this case asking a witness the same series of questions, perhaps from a slightly different angle, regarding the same accused. It appears to me that we would risk having essentially ganging up on a witness on a particular issue. I think the example that Mr. Radovic gave about the black flag was a very legitimate line of questioning. We don't doubt that. But I do recall him asking a series of questions dealing only with whether or not this -- how this witness new Papic, how this witness could identify Papic. These questions, it seems to me, are more appropriately given by the counsel representing Papic and I think they were, and then from a different angle, counsel number 2 does the same thing and from a third angle counsel number 3 does it again, and I think our concern, while we don't want to unduly limit legitimate cross-examination, and I think it is important for credibility of witnesses to be adequately and thoroughly tested, there's no doubt about that, but I think there comes a point or a line beyond that that I think it becomes -- I won't say witness harassment, but it just goes on too long and it becomes unfair to some of these witnesses who have to sit here for sometimes hours enduring it. I am looking for some way, I think, to have a legitimate balance between the witness's -- frankly, the witness's rights not to be harangued by one Defence attorney after another coming from different angles on essentially the same topic and the legitimate rights of the accused to have credibility tested. It seems to me that that line might legitimately be drawn in this case with making some sort of a rule that would limit questions that solely pertained to a Defendant to the lawyer representing that accused and, of course, there would be some flexibility because sometimes that line isn't so clear, as in the black flag example, but we do request that the Court give some consideration to establishing some limitation; otherwise, I fear that we're going to have some problems with witnesses being harassed and feeling that they're being harassed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The danger of a rule is that you do injustice in the particular case, and I would have thought, with respect, that the right answer is that it's for the Court to determine in each case where the line is drawn between legitimate cross-examination and what becomes repetitive and oppressive to the witness, and in each case, that will have to be judged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Here I would take a different approach from my colleague, but you see here, this reflects the approach, the common law approach, and the typical continental European approach where we like principles, rules, and I think this also applies to Croatia, former Yugoslavia, where we have different legal training. I wonder whether we could probably try to think of a solution. We are here -- we are breaking new ground, of course, again. We can't apply either Croatian or British or Italian or French or Zambian law or American law, we have to think of law, a set of rules to be applied in the light of the basic principles of our Statute, namely, the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial. So therefore, we probably could think of some sort of broad guidelines and then, within those guidelines, which we would try to offer maybe next week, we could, on a case-by-case basis then decide if and when objections are raised according to the pragmatic approach suggested by Judge May. I wonder whether we could combine those two approaches, a sort of principled and pragmatic approach, but I agree with the Prosecution, that this is a difficult area. We will try to come to some sort of wise and balanced solution which, of course, should never affect or curtail the rights of the Defence. May I suggest we now move on to our next legal counsel, Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I have no further questions, not because of the Prosecutor's remark, but because we have truly exhausted all the questions I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other counsel? No other counsel is going to ask questions? I wonder whether the Prosecutor would like to re-examine the witness? Re-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, you were questioned a moment ago as to your knowledge of the Ustashe. Could you specify to the Court what this word "Ustashe" stands for for you, what it means?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: For me, these are criminals. That's what the word means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through whom or how did you get to hear about the Ustashe?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard from the former war, the Second World War, I read in books what they had done, how they had done it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1943, so you're too young to have experienced that time. Did you hear about the Ustashe through your parents?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I read history when I went to school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you saw this black flag flying from Dragan Papic's house, you associated that flag with what you knew about the Ustashe, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Mr. President. My apologies, Mr. President, two further questions, two additional questions. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic asked a question of Mr. Rizvanovic, and in answer to it, you said that you didn't meet with any representative of the Office of the Prosecutor between yesterday's hearing and this morning. I would like to clarify this. I don't know whether the transcript or the translation that I received was absolutely faithful. But I had the feeling that you said "No," that you didn't meet anybody in between. That's not right, is it, because you did meet with somebody, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is as follows: This morning, before the hearing began, did you meet with a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to say that. When I was coming here, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, when you were coming here this morning.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, would you mind looking at the photograph again? Could you once again, so as to avoid any ambiguity or any problem, any further problems, could you tell us in which house you were staying with your family prior to the 16th of April, 1993? Could you show it using the pointer?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the cemetery, this is this house, this is that house. I was in this house next to the wood, on the left side. Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the house which stands closest to the woods. Were there any other houses between yours and the forest?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a house here, next to ours (indicating).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he's not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rizvanovic. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, allow me one question. Do you intend to ask the witness whether he can identify any accused? I was thinking of Dragan Papic because he spoke about Dragan Papic. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, we could ask this of the witness. Of course, the Tribunal will be able to ascertain to which extent -- the witness is full of emotions and has problems in identifying people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, can you hear me? Do you know where the accused are sitting in this courtroom? It might be necessary to locate everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware. It might be better not to put the question that way. Do not ask where the accused are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, I didn't specify, I asked Mr. Rizvanovic whether he knew where the accused were. I do want to make sure that there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You could ask whether he recognises anyone in this courtroom no matter where that person may sit or stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, do you recognise anybody in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name the person you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind pointing him to us?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at him. Over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's not enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you said that you were looking at him. But could you use your finger, point to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And say where he's sitting or standing.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: He's sitting, he's sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is he sitting in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe his physical aspect?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has a beard, he had a beard before, and a little moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions from the Court. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. I see no objection. Mr. Rizvanovic, you may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, we have another 15 minutes. We could possibly use them to let the next witness in, or we're going to have a break now? What do you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, our next witness is listed as Witness No. 3 on page 6 of our filing entitled "Prosecution Submission of Information Helpful for Trial," dated August 19, and this is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: On page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This is a protected witness who has requested face protection, voice protection, and pseudonym protection. We have discussed this matter with the Defence counsel, and they do not oppose this request. So at this time, we would request that those protective measures be granted for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And it would be Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand from the technicians they would prefer to ask to take a break now. It would facilitate the taking of the necessary measures for the protection of the witness. So I suggest that we now break, and we come back in 30 minutes. So a quarter past eleven sharp with the witness in here. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please stand and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone wasn't on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is it on now? Could you please read it again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But we can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear him. Maybe, meanwhile, the Prosecutor could show us his name on a slip of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll tender this to the witness, to the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm now tendering a slip of paper with the witness's name on it to the usher for showing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Does the microphone work now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, the technician has come and fixed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness A. I would like, again, to ask you to stand and read once again the solemn declaration because we don't have it on our transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. WITNESS A Examined by Mr. Moskowitz:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to inform you again that you have been granted the protective measures that you have requested. I'll be asking you a series of questions, and I would like to ask you that if a response to any of my questions would, in any way, you feel, tend to identify you in some way, please feel free to say that before responding. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court how old you are, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you and your family are not originally from Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we're not. We're from eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you family settle in the village of Ahmici? Could you tell us that date?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was in the month of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family, at that time, were refugees from the Foca area?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my wife's family was from Foca, and my family originated from a place which I can't tell you the name of now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us briefly what was happening in Foca that rendered your family refugees from that area?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the houses of my family in eastern Bosnia were burned down due to the Chetnik Serbian aggression, my family was driven away and they had to seek refuge in the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned your family, and I don't want you to mention any names, but can you give us an idea of what your family consisted of at that time, the relationships?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean where we lived in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess I'm asking you to give us an idea of what your family consisted of at that time. Did it consist of a father, a mother, a wife, and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a father, a mother, and three brothers. I also had a wife and a child, and my wife had her father, her mother, and two brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this the family you were referring to, these group of people who settled in Ahmici as refugees in or about November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In November 1992, my mother and my two younger brothers, who were twins, arrived, and in the other house, my mother-in-law, my father-in-law and my wife, with our small child, settled, and one of their youngest sons; and in a house nearby, my wife's brother, with his wife and child, settled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your family settled basically in two separate houses in the Ahmici area in '92; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these houses close together, or were they in different parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were close to one another, some 40 metres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this time, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in eastern Bosnia, in the area of eastern Bosnia on the mountain of Grebak near eastern Vojvodina. I was in the war theatre. I was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were fighting for the Bosnia army on the Serbian front.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a time that you, I suppose like many other soldiers, were given permission to go and have some rest and relaxation or take some leave from the front and visit the family? Did that occur during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the war theatre for a long time. I hadn't been in Central Bosnia; I didn't know where my family was. First, they were somewhere near Sivrino Selo. When I arrived there, they had gone, and I learned that they had moved to the hamlet of Ahmici, and I found them there. That was in 1993, in February, towards the end of February, because when I arrived there, I found them there in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Sivrino Selo. That's a small village right outside Vitez, between Vitez and Ahmici on the valley road; is that right, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in that village for the first time then. I'd never been to Vitez. I came there for the first time. I asked people where Sivrino Selo was; they told me. And when I arrived there, they said that my family had moved to the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall about what time of year this was or what year this was when you were granted leave from the front to go and visit your family? Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the month of February. It was cold, there was snow. At least there was snow on the front. It was cold, it was winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this be in the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk a little bit, if we could, about the technicalities of leaving a war front in Bosnia in 1992 or 1993 for a Bosnian soldier at that time. I take it that while you were at the front, you had a weapon that you were provided for use in defending the Bosnia territories from the Serbs. Would that be a good assumption, you did have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had weapons, I had an automatic gun which I had there, and I had to leave there when I had -- when I went home. It was more needed on the front-line. We were not allowed to take our weapons with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you left to go on home leave sometime in February of '93, you had to leave your weapon behind you at the front; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that normal practice in the army at that time, for soldiers going home on leave to go home without their weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the usual practice, because the army did not have enough weapons, so no one could take their weapons with them. This was the period when the army had more soldiers than weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was there any concern as well that if soldiers took their weapons home with them, they might be stopped at checkpoints along the way and their weapons taken from them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some cases. Some of my fellow fighters from our unit had complained earlier that at the checkpoints near Kiseljak, their weapons had been taken away, pistols, guns, when they carried them with them. Especially in January 1993, if they went, there were allegedly some clashes in Central Bosnia, and everybody said that weapons shouldn't be carried and that it's very hard to pass through in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we talk about these checkpoints, was it your -- what was your understanding as to who was manning these checkpoints where weapons were being removed from soldiers returning from the front?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned that your family had, in fact, moved into two different houses. Close together but, nevertheless, two different houses in Ahmici. When you went to Ahmici and found your family, which house did you stay at? Maybe you can identify that by describing the family members you were with, not by name but just by relationship.

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I forgot to tell you earlier that there were actually three houses, not two, because my wife's brother was in the third house, and I arrived in a house which was owned by a certain Enver Ahmic, and that house was inhabited by my wife with her child, my father-in-law, my mother-in-law, and their son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it your father and mother were in a different house close by?

utterances.speaker: ESAD RIZVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were nearby in a house close to the nearby woods. I don't know who the owner of the house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would ask the usher to place on the ELMO an exhibit, which I'm sure the Court is familiar with; it is the blow-up of that part of the village of Ahmici. I guess my concern a little bit is whether this will compromise his protection and seek the guidance of the Court as to best to do this without compromising protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you going to ask the witness to identify his house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It will be necessary for me to have him identify several houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. But since the transcripts are confidential. (DISCUSSION WITH REGISTRAR OFF THE RECORD)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar has suggested that we should go into a closed session for a few minutes so that the public gallery will not see anything, not even this photograph. (Closed session) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Whereupon proceedings adjourned at 5.07 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of August, 1998, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: Pages 531 to 632 redacted - in closed session
